q: Which of these cannot travel through a vacuum?
x: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium to carry its vibrations. Light, radio waves and X-rays are electromagnetic waves and travel through empty space.

q: An FM radio station broadcasts at 100 MHz. Radio waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. The wavelength of the waves is:
x: λ = v/f = 3 × 10⁸/(100 × 10⁶) = 3 m. Using 100 Hz instead of 100 MHz gives 3 × 10⁶ m; the other values are prefix slips.

q: When a wave passes from one medium into another, the quantity that stays the same is its:
x: The frequency is fixed by the source, so it does not change at the boundary. The speed changes with the medium, and since v = fλ the wavelength changes with it.

q: Crests of a water wave travel 12 m in 3 s, and neighbouring crests are 0.5 m apart. The frequency of the wave is:
x: v = 12/3 = 4 m s⁻¹ and λ = 0.5 m, so f = v/λ = 4/0.5 = 8 Hz. Multiplying v by λ gives 2; dividing the distance 12 m directly by λ gives 24.

q: Mechanical transverse waves cannot travel through:
x: A transverse wave needs the medium to resist sideways (shear) displacement. A gas has no such rigidity, so only longitudinal waves travel through it. Strings, solids and water surfaces can carry transverse waves.

q: A small source sends sound out equally in all directions. At 2 m from the source the amplitude of the air vibrations is 4 μm. Ignoring absorption, the amplitude at 8 m from the source is:
x: Intensity ∝ 1/r² (the power spreads over 4πr²) and intensity ∝ amplitude², so amplitude ∝ 1/r: 4 × 2/8 = 1 μm. Applying the inverse square law to the amplitude gives 0.25 μm.

q: In the time a particle of the medium completes one full vibration, a progressive wave travels a distance of:
x: One vibration takes one period T, and in time T the wave moves vT = λ, one wavelength. Four times the amplitude is the distance the particle itself moves in one vibration, not the wave.

q: Laplace's correction changes Newton's formula for the speed of sound in a gas by a factor of:
x: Newton: v = √(P/ρ). Laplace replaced P by γP (adiabatic changes), so v = √(γP/ρ), larger by a factor √γ (about 1.18 for air). Multiplying the speed by γ itself forgets the square root.

q: At the same temperature and pressure, the speed of sound in humid air, compared with dry air, is:
o: Smaller, because humid air is denser
The same, because the pressure is the same
Smaller, because water vapour absorbs sound
Greater, because humid air is less dense
x: Water vapour (molar mass 18 g mol⁻¹) is lighter than dry air (about 29 g mol⁻¹), so humid air is less dense, and v = √(γP/ρ) is greater. Thinking moist air is 'heavier' gives the reverse.

q: An electric bell rings inside a glass jar. As the air is pumped out, the sound heard gets fainter, although the bell is still seen to vibrate. This shows that:
o: Sound needs a material medium to travel
Glass does not let sound through
Sound travels faster in a vacuum
x: The bell is still vibrating, but with less and less air to carry the vibrations less sound reaches us: sound needs a medium. The sound was heard through the glass at first, so glass does transmit sound.

q: A ship's sonar sends a sound pulse straight down. The echo from the sea bed returns after 2 s. Sound travels at 1500 m s⁻¹ in sea water. The depth of the sea is:
x: In 2 s the pulse travels 1500 × 2 = 3000 m, down and back up, so the depth is 3000/2 = 1500 m. Forgetting the return trip gives 3000 m.

q: A gas has pressure 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, density 1.4 kg m⁻³ and γ = 1.4. Using Laplace's formula, the speed of sound in it is about:
x: v = √(γP/ρ) = √(1.4 × 10⁵/1.4) = √(10⁵) ≈ 316 m s⁻¹. Newton's formula without γ gives √(10⁵/1.4) ≈ 267 m s⁻¹.

q: The speed of sound in a gas does NOT depend on the:
o: Ratio of specific heats γ of the gas
x: v = √(γP/ρ) = √(γRT/M) contains no frequency, so all frequencies travel at the same speed (otherwise music heard from far away would arrive out of step). Temperature, molar mass and γ all change v.

q: Sound travels at 300 m s⁻¹ in a gas of density 1.5 kg m⁻³ at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Using Laplace's formula, the ratio of specific heats γ of the gas is:
x: From v = √(γP/ρ), γ = v²ρ/P = 9 × 10⁴ × 1.5/10⁵ = 1.35. Inverting the ratio gives 0.74; 1.16 is √1.35; 1.67 is the value for a monatomic gas, not this one.

q: According to the principle of superposition, when two waves overlap at a point, the resultant displacement there is the:
o: Product of the displacements due to the separate waves
Vector sum of the displacements due to the separate waves
Larger of the two separate displacements
Difference of the two amplitudes, whatever the phases
x: Superposition: the resultant displacement at each instant is the vector (signed) sum of the individual displacements. Whether this gives reinforcement or cancellation depends on the phases.

q: Two coherent sources vibrate in phase and send out waves of wavelength λ. Destructive interference occurs at points where the path difference is (n = 0, 1, 2, …):
x: A path difference of an odd number of half wavelengths, (n + ½)λ, brings crest onto trough, so the waves cancel. A whole number of wavelengths, nλ, gives constructive interference.

q: Two tuning forks of 340 Hz and 345 Hz are sounded together. The time between two successive loud sounds (waxings) is:
x: Beat frequency = 345 − 340 = 5 Hz, so there are 5 loud sounds per second, one every 1/5 = 0.2 s. Giving the beat frequency 5 as a time is the usual slip.

q: Noise-cancelling headphones reduce steady background noise by producing a sound wave that, compared with the noise, has:
o: The same frequency and amplitude, and is in phase
The same frequency and amplitude, but is half a cycle out of phase
Twice the frequency and the same amplitude
The same frequency, in phase, but a much larger amplitude
x: For destructive interference the added wave must meet each compression with a rarefaction: same frequency and amplitude, phase difference π (half a cycle). An in-phase wave would make the noise louder.

q: A tuning fork of unknown frequency gives 3 beats per second with a 400 Hz fork and 5 beats per second with a 408 Hz fork. Its frequency is:
x: From the first fork the frequency is 397 or 403 Hz; from the second, 403 or 413 Hz. Only 403 Hz fits both (check: 403 − 400 = 3 and 408 − 403 = 5). 397 Hz would give 11 beats with the 408 Hz fork.

q: Two coherent waves interfere. At points of complete destructive interference there is no energy. This is because the energy is:
o: Redistributed, being greater at the maxima, so the total is conserved
Converted into heat at the minima
Reflected back to the sources from the minima
x: Interference does not create or destroy energy: the intensity is zero at the minima and four times that of one wave at the maxima, so the energy is only redistributed and the total is unchanged.

q: Beats are produced by the superposition of two sound waves that:
o: Have slightly different frequencies and travel in the same direction
Have the same frequency and travel in opposite directions
Have the same frequency and are always in phase
Have very different frequencies and amplitudes
x: Two waves of slightly different frequency drift in and out of phase, so the loudness rises and falls: beats. Equal frequencies travelling in opposite directions form a stationary wave instead.

q: In a stationary wave of wavelength λ, the distance between a node and the next antinode is:
x: Neighbouring nodes are λ/2 apart, and an antinode lies midway between them, so node to next antinode is λ/4. λ/2 is the node-to-node distance.

q: A pipe 0.85 m long is open at both ends. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. Its fundamental frequency is:
x: An open pipe has antinodes at both ends, so L = λ/2 for the fundamental: λ = 1.7 m and f = 340/1.7 = 200 Hz. The closed-pipe formula v/4L gives 100 Hz; 600 Hz is the third harmonic.

q: An air column in a pipe closed at one end can resonate at:
x: A closed end must be a node and an open end an antinode, so the length must be an odd number of quarter wavelengths, L = (2n − 1)λ/4, giving only odd harmonics. All harmonics occur in a pipe open at both ends.

q: A string 0.8 m long, of mass per unit length 0.01 kg m⁻¹, is fixed at both ends and stretched by a tension of 64 N. Its fundamental frequency is:
x: Wave speed v = √(F/μ) = √(64/0.01) = √6400 = 80 m s⁻¹; fundamental f₁ = v/2L = 80/1.6 = 50 Hz. Using v/L gives 100 Hz; forgetting the square root gives 4000 Hz.

q: The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is 120 Hz. The frequency of its second overtone is:
x: For a string fixed at both ends the overtones are 2f₁, 3f₁, …; the second overtone is the third harmonic, 3 × 120 = 360 Hz. Taking the second overtone as the second harmonic gives 240 Hz.

q: A 500 Hz tuning fork is held over a tube closed at its lower end. Resonance is heard when the air column is 17 cm long and again when it is 51 cm long. Ignoring end correction, the speed of sound is:
x: Successive resonances in a closed tube differ by λ/2: 51 − 17 = 34 cm, so λ = 68 cm and v = fλ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m s⁻¹ (check: the first resonance L = λ/4 = 17 cm). Taking 34 cm as λ gives 170 m s⁻¹.

q: The Doppler effect is the apparent change in the:
o: Frequency of a wave caused by relative motion of the source and the observer
Speed of a wave when it enters a new medium
Amplitude of a wave as it spreads out from its source
Wavelength of a wave when it is reflected from a surface
x: The Doppler effect is the change in the observed frequency (and pitch) when the source and the observer move relative to each other. A change of speed in a new medium is refraction.

q: A car sounding its horn and a cyclist ahead of it move in the same direction along a straight road, both at 10 m s⁻¹, in still air. The frequency heard by the cyclist is:
o: Equal to the frequency of the horn
Higher than the frequency of the horn
Lower than the frequency of the horn
Higher at first and then lower
x: f′ = f(v − u_o)/(v − u_s) with u_o = u_s = 10 m s⁻¹, so f′ = f. There is no relative motion between source and observer, so there is no Doppler shift.

q: Doctors use the Doppler effect with ultrasound to measure the:
o: Speed of blood flowing in an artery
x: Ultrasound reflected from moving blood cells comes back with a shifted frequency, and the size of the shift gives the speed of the blood flow. Electrical activity of the heart is recorded by an ECG, not by ultrasound.

q: A car moves at 20 m s⁻¹ straight towards a high wall, sounding a horn of frequency 500 Hz. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. The frequency of the echo heard by the driver is:
x: The wall receives f₁ = 500 × 340/(340 − 20) = 531.25 Hz and reflects it as a fixed source; the driver moving towards it hears f₂ = 531.25 × (340 + 20)/340 = 562.5 Hz (in one step: 500 × 360/320). 531.25 Hz is only the frequency at the wall.

q: A source of sound moves steadily towards a stationary observer in still air. Compared with when the source is at rest, the sound reaching the observer has:
o: A shorter wavelength and the same speed
A shorter wavelength and a greater speed
A longer wavelength and the same speed
The same wavelength and a greater speed
x: The speed of sound is set by the air, not by the source, so it is unchanged. The moving source crowds the waves together in front of it, so the wavelength is shorter and the frequency higher.

q: A stationary source emits sound of 400 Hz in still air, where sound travels at 320 m s⁻¹. An observer moves straight towards the source at 16 m s⁻¹. The wavelength of the sound around the observer and the frequency he hears are:
x: The source is still, so the wavelength in the air is unchanged: λ = 320/400 = 0.80 m. The observer meets the waves at 320 + 16 = 336 m s⁻¹, so f′ = 336/0.80 = 420 Hz. Dividing 320 by 420 wrongly shortens the wavelength to 0.76 m.
